unesco.title: Hayachine Kagura
unesco.description: In the fourteenth or fifteenth century, when the people of Iwate Prefecture in the northern part of mainland Japan worshipped Mt. Hayachine as a deity, they began a tradition of folk performance that continues to enliven the Great Festival of the Hayachine Shrine held in Hanamaki City on the first day of August. The Hayachine Kagura is a series of masked dances accompanied by drum, cymbals and flute: six ritual dances begin the performance; five dances recount stories of the deities and medieval Japanese history, and a final dance features a performer dressed as a ''shishi,'' an imaginary lion-like creature representing the Hayachine deity himself. Originally danced by holy officers of the Shrine to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity and bless the people, the Hayachine Kagura is now performed by representatives of the entire community, who take pride in their distinctive culture. To transmit and display the ritual is to reconfirm a sense of identity within the group and to contribute to the continuity of an important tradition. Its enactment also commemorates events from Japanese history and celebrates one of the mountain deities worshipped throughout the country.

profile.name: Hayachine Kagura
profile.tagline: A series of twelve masked ritual dances performed at Hayachine Shrine, Japan.
profile.insight: On August 1st, a performer dons a shishi mask to embody the mountain deity of Mount Hayachine, concluding a five-hour cycle of twelve ritual dances that have been performed since the 14th or 15th century.
profile.profile: Hayachine Kagura is a series of twelve masked ritual dances performed annually at the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate, Japan. The cycle begins with six ritualistic dances, followed by five dances depicting medieval Japanese history and deities, and concludes with a performance by a shishi, a lion-like creature representing the mountain god. Originally performed by shrine officials, the tradition is now maintained by lay community members as a vital expression of local identity.
profile.profile_long: The Hayachine Kagura is a ritual performance tradition centered at the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate Prefecture. Dating back to the 14th or 15th century, the practice emerged from the worship of Mount Hayachine as a divine entity. Historically, these dances were the exclusive domain of holy shrine officers, who performed them to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity and to bestow blessings upon the local population. Over time, the performance transitioned into a community-led tradition, now maintained by lay practitioners who take pride in their cultural heritage. The full cycle of Hayachine Kagura consists of twelve distinct dances and spans approximately five hours. The sequence is structured into three thematic parts: the first six dances are strictly ritualistic, the next five recount medieval Japanese history and the stories of various deities, and the final dance features a performer dressed as a shishi, an imaginary lion-like creature that serves as the personification of the mountain god. The dancers wear masks throughout the performance, which is accompanied by an ensemble playing drums, cymbals, and flutes. While the primary performance occurs annually on August 1st at the Hayachine Shrine, the dances are also presented at other times of the year and in various locations throughout the Iwate Prefecture. These performances, often referred to as 'discipleship' shows, serve to transmit the tradition and reinforce the collective identity of the community. Scholars have noted potential influences from the practices of the yamabushi—Buddhist ascetics who lived in the mountains—and have explored possible historical connections between this kagura and the development of Noh theater. In 2009, UNESCO recognized the significance of this tradition by inscribing it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, acknowledging its role in celebrating mountain deities and preserving Japanese history.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition originated in the 14th or 15th century in the Iwate Prefecture, rooted in the worship of Mount Hayachine. It was historically performed by shrine officers and is believed to have been influenced by the practices of yamabushi, mountain-dwelling Buddhist ascetics. Scholars continue to investigate its potential links to the history of Noh theater.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance consists of twelve dances, with dancers wearing masks. The final dance features a performer as a shishi, a lion-like creature. The full cycle lasts five hours. Specific footwork and gesture techniques are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed by an ensemble using drums, cymbals, and flutes. This musical accompaniment supports the twelve ritual dances.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear masks during the dances. The primary setting is the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate, where the performance takes place on August 1st, though it is also performed in other locations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dances are performed in honor of Seoritsu, the tutelary deity of Mount Hayachine. The performance serves to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity, bless the people, and reconfirm the identity of the community.
sections.regional_variants: While the main tradition is at Hayachine Shrine, 'discipleship' shows are performed throughout the Iwate Prefecture, though rarely as the full twelve-dance cycle.
sections.lineage: The tradition is a type of Kagura, a category of ritual dance in Shinto ceremonies.
